'''Geraint Francis Lewis, [[Learned Society of Wales|FLSW]]''' (born 14 March 1969) is a [[Welsh people|Welsh]] [[astrophysics|astrophysicist]], best known for his work on [[dark energy]], [[gravitational lensing]] and [[galactic cannibalism]].<ref>
{{cite web|title=Personal webpage|url=https://www.geraintflewis.com}}
</ref>
Lewis is a [[professor]] of astrophysics (teaching and research) at the Sydney Institute for Astronomy, part of the [[University of Sydney]]'s School of Physics. He is head of the Gravitational Astrophysics Group. He was previously the associate head for research at the School of Physics, and held an [[Australian Research Council]] Future Fellowship between 2011 and 2015.

Lewis won the 2016 [[Walter Boas Medal]] in recognition of excellence in research in physics.<ref>{{cite web|title=Walter Boas Medal|url=http://aip.org.au/medals-awards-and-prizes/walter-boas-medal/|website=Australian Institute of Physics|accessdate=6 March 2018|archive-date=21 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190921012931/https://aip.org.au/medals-awards-and-prizes/walter-boas-medal/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2021, he was awarded the David Allen Prize of the [[Astronomical Society of Australia]] for exceptional achievement in astronomy communication.<ref>{{cite web|title=David Allen Prize|url=https://www.scienceinpublic.com.au/media-releases/asa-awards-2021}}</ref> In April 2020, he was elected a Fellow of the [[Learned Society of Wales]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Learned Society of Wales welcomes 45 New Fellows|url=https://www.learnedsociety.wales/forty-five-new-fellows-for-the-learned-society-of-wales/|website=Learned Society of Wales|date=29 April 2020|accessdate=30 April 2020}}</ref> He is also an elected fellow of the [[Royal Society of New South Wales]].

Until the end of 2020, Lewis held the position of deputy director of the Sydney Informatics Hub,<ref>
{{cite web|title=Sydney Informatics Hub|url=https://www.sydney.edu.au/research/facilities/sydney-informatics-hub.html}}</ref> a Core Research Facility<ref>
{{cite web|title=Core Research Facility|url=https://www.sydney.edu.au/dam/corporate/documents/research/crf-brochure.pdf}}</ref> of the [[University of Sydney]].

== Education ==
Originally from [[Wales]], Lewis was born in [[Neath]] and raised in [[Seven Sisters, Neath Port Talbot|Seven Sisters]] and [[Crynant]], completing schooling at [[Llangatwg Comprehensive]] and [[Neath Tertiary College]]. He completed his first degree at the [[University of London]] and [[PhD]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]'s [[Institute of Astronomy, Cambridge|Institute of Astronomy]]. He has worked in the [[State University of New York]], the [[University of Victoria]] in [[Canada]], and the [[University of Washington]] in [[Seattle]]. After [[research fellow|research positions]] in the [[US]] and Canada, he then became a research astronomer at the [[Anglo-Australian Observatory]] in 2000. In 2002, Lewis joined the University of Sydney, where he is currently the head of the Gravitational Astrophysics Group.

== Research fields ==
Lewis undertakes a broad spectrum of research in [[astronomy]] and [[cosmology]].<ref>
{{cite web|title=Geraint F. Lewis: Research|url=https://www.geraintflewis.com/research}}</ref>
On the largest scales, his program involves looking at the influence of [[dark energy]] and [[dark matter]] on the [[cosmic evolution|evolution]] and [[ultimate fate of the universe]].
Another aspect of Lewis's research uses the phenomenon of gravitational lensing to probe the nature and distribution of the pervasive dark matter, and employing individual stars to [[magnify]] the hearts of [[quasar]]s, the most luminous objects in the universe.

Closer to home, Lewis's research focuses upon galactic cannibalism, where small [[dwarf galaxies]] are torn apart by the much more massive [[Milky Way]] and [[Andromeda Galaxy]]. Using [[telescope]]s from around the world, including the 10-m [[Keck telescope]] in [[Hawaii]], he has mapped the tell-tale signs of [[tidal force|tidal disruption and destruction]], providing important clues to how large [[galaxies]] have grown over time.

== Publications ==
As of August 2020, Lewis has published more than 400 [[scientific articles]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Publications at SAO/NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS)|url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/public-libraries/d8M2nfxrSEexxYXKSHJUjg}}</ref>
numerous articles in the popular press,  and three popular science books.
* ''Where did the Universe come from? And other cosmic questions'' by [[Chris Ferrie]] and Geraint F. Lewis, SourceBooks (Chicago), (Sept 2021,{{ISBN|978-1728238814}})
* ''The Cosmic Revolutionary's Handbook: or how to beat the Big Bang'' by Luke A. Barnes and Geraint F. Lewis, Cambridge University Press (Feb 2020, {{ISBN|978-1108762090}})
* ''A Fortunate Universe: Life in a finely tuned cosmos'' by Geraint F. Lewis and Luke A. Barnes, Cambridge University Press (Oct 2016, {{ISBN|978-1107156616}})
*''Dark Matter in Astroparticle and Particle Physics - Proceedings of the 6th International Heidelberg Conference'', World Scientific Publishing Company, Australia, 2007, {{ISBN|978-981-281-434-0}}<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.worldscibooks.com/physics/6838.html|title=''DARK MATTER IN ASTROPARTICLE AND PARTICLE PHYSICS - Proceedings of the 6th International Heidelberg Conference'' from World Scientific Books webpage|publisher=}}</ref>

==Public outreach==
Lewis is noted for his public speaking about astronomy on radio and at public events.<ref>{{cite web|title=Media Appearances|url=https://www.geraintflewis.com/media}}</ref>
He was appointed Patron of [[Macarthur Astronomical Society]] in February 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.macastro.org.au/mas/index.php/about-us/information/our-patron |title=Our Patron - Macarthur Astronomical Society |website=www.macastro.org.au |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314130316/http://www.macastro.org.au/mas/index.php/about-us/information/our-patron |archive-date=2018-03-14}}</ref>
With his colleague, Luke Barnes, he regularly discusses astronomy, cosmology and physics at his YouTube channel Alas Lewis & Barnes.<ref>
{{cite web|title=Alas Lewis & Barnes|website=[[YouTube]]|url=https://www.youtube.com/c/AlasLewisAndBarnes}}
</ref>
